content: Acid etching of tooth surfaces has been a standard procedure in orthodontics since the 1960s to enhance the bonding of orthodontic brackets to enamel. Over the past five decades, various types of etching agents and techniques have been developed. Despite the extensive research on this topic, there remains a lack of consensus regarding the clinical effectiveness of different etching materials and methods. The objective of this study was to compare the effects of different dental etching agents and techniques on the bonding of fixed orthodontic appliances. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple electronic databases, including the Cochrane Oral Health Group's Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Chinese Biomedical Literature Database, the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, and the National Institutes of Health Clinical Trials Registry. The search was updated to the most recent issues, and no restrictions were placed on language or publication date. Additionally, a handsearching group reviewed journals as part of the Cochrane Worldwide Handsearching Programme. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared different etching materials or techniques for bonding fixed orthodontic brackets to incisors, canines, and premolars in both children and adults. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were performed independently and in duplicate by two review authors. Disagreements were resolved through discussion, and corresponding authors of included studies were contacted for additional information when necessary. Thirteen studies involving 417 participants and 7184 teeth/brackets were included in the review. Of these, two studies (15%) were assessed as having a low risk of bias, ten studies (77%) as having a high risk of bias, and one study (8%) as having an unclear risk of bias. When comparing self-etching primers (SEPs) to conventional etching systems, eleven studies were identified. However, only five of these studies reported data at the participant level, while the others reported at the tooth level, which did not account for the paired nature of the data. A meta-analysis of these five studies, with follow-up periods ranging from 5 to 37 months, provided low-quality evidence. The results were inconclusive regarding whether there is a difference in bond failure rates between SEPs and conventional etching systems (risk ratio 1.14; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.75 to 1.73; 221 participants). The wide confidence interval included both no effect and potential benefits or harms. Subgroup analysis did not reveal any differences between split-mouth and parallel study designs. No data were available to assess outcomes such as decalcification, participant satisfaction, or cost-effectiveness. One study reported on decalcification, but only at the tooth level. Two studies compared different SEPs. Both studies reported bond failure rates, and one also reported on decalcification. However, as the outcomes were reported only at the tooth level, there was insufficient data to determine whether one SEP was superior to another in terms of any of the outcomes assessed in this review. No eligible studies were found that evaluated different etching materials (e.g., phosphoric acid, polyacrylic acid, maleic acid), concentrations, or etching times. In conclusion, the evidence available was of low quality and insufficient to determine whether there is a difference in bond failure rates between SEPs and conventional etching systems for bonding fixed orthodontic appliances over a follow-up period of 5 to 37 months. Additionally, there was insufficient data to draw conclusions about the superiority of SEPs or conventional etching systems in terms of decalcification, participant satisfaction, or cost-effectiveness. Similarly, no conclusions could be made regarding the superiority of different etching materials, concentrations, or etching times, or the relative effectiveness of different SEPs. Further well-designed randomized controlled trials are needed to provide more robust evidence to address these clinical questions.
